name: Gluten-free diet
short: Heavy metals: higher blood mercury, lead and urine arsenic on the diet (US survey); arsenic rose, then normalised, in coeliac children. Coeliac children: low folate, calcium, vitamin D intake.
text: Heavy metals: in a US population survey (the abstract does not give ages), the 115 participants on a gluten-free diet had higher blood mercury, lead and cadmium than people not on the diet, and higher urine arsenic (measured in 32 of them), and the mercury, lead and arsenic differences held in people without coeliac disease; the authors say the long-term effects of this accumulation need study. In a prospective study of 35 children aged 2 to 18 with newly diagnosed coeliac disease, urinary arsenic rose after 6 months on the diet, at levels the authors say were well below acutely toxic concentrations, with the clinical impact of chronic exposure unknown; in the 21 children followed to 12 months, it had returned to baseline. A study of 30 people with coeliac disease (ages not given in the abstract) found blood mercury about four times higher in those following the diet. Nutrition in children with coeliac disease (a different population, for whom the diet is the standard treatment): reviews report that intakes of folate, magnesium, zinc and selenium may fall on the diet and that imbalances such as too little fibre, iron, vitamin D and calcium may be made worse; in 48 Polish children on a strict gluten-free diet, serum vitamin B1 and folic acid were lower than in 50 children without coeliac disease, serum calcium was lower although within normal ranges, and calcium, folic acid and vitamin D intakes were below recommendations but did not differ significantly from those of the children without coeliac disease. Bone and growth in children with coeliac disease (in whom the disease itself can lower bone density): spine bone density rose on the diet in 24 children followed for about a year (Z-score from -1.36 to -0.23); 91 symptom-free children on the diet for years had normal or higher forearm bone density than a healthy population, but smaller bone size, and the adolescent girls had lower than normal bone mineral content; in a cross-sectional study, 3 of 31 children on the diet had low spine bone density; and in Kuwait, 31% of 77 children with coeliac disease had stunted growth despite following the diet. On the other side, a meta-analysis of 45 studies in people with coeliac disease found that body mass index rose on the diet but that the diet did not increase the risk of becoming overweight or obese, especially in children. Other populations (the abstracts do not give ages): in a double-blind trial in 16 inpatients with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder who had raised antigliadin antibodies but did not have coeliac disease, all eating gluten-free meals and randomised to a daily gluten or rice flour shake for 5 weeks, adverse effects were similar between the groups, and gut adverse effects improved more in the gluten-free group. In 98 people with newly diagnosed coeliac disease, the share meeting criteria for metabolic syndrome rose from 2% at diagnosis to 29.5% after 12 months on the diet (a before-and-after study with no comparison group). Without a medical diagnosis: a review says some parents adopt gluten-free diets for their children and describes detrimental effects of going gluten free, including loss of dietary fibre, deficiencies in minerals and vitamins, and potential heavy-metal exposure. Autism: in a 1991 study of seven people with autism given the diet, the authors felt it seemed to add to social isolation for these patients and families; the autism trial abstracts cited on the autism page report no adverse-event data. No bone density data were found for children without coeliac disease on the diet. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
